name: Rajesh
definition: Rajesh is a composite portrait of a grape farmer and borewell contractor in Nandi taluk, Chikkaballapur district, navigating the twin pressures of groundwater depletion and the district's proximity to Bengaluru. He embodies the resilience and economic calculation of families in the bayalu seeme who farm water-intensive crops while selling drilling services to their neighbours, caught between horticultural ambition and hydrological reality.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Rajesh owns four acres of grape vines near Nandi town, mostly Bangalore Blue variety destined for the Bengaluru wholesale markets and a small patch of wine grapes contracted to a winery near Doddaballapur. His day begins at five-thirty with drip-irrigation checks; by eight he is usually out on a borewell-drilling job, operating a truck-mounted rig he bought on loan three years ago. Drilling work has become his main income as neighbours chase deeper water tables, some borewells now reaching four hundred feet with no guarantee of yield. He charges by the foot and by the hour, earning between twelve and twenty thousand rupees per borewell depending on geology and depth. Grape farming is riskier: a good harvest in March-April can net him eighty thousand from his four acres, but late rains or a price crash at the Chikkaballapur market can halve that. His wife keeps accounts and negotiates with the commission agents. The drilling rig needs diesel, spare bits and a helper's daily wage; the vines need fertiliser, pesticides and casual labour for pruning and harvest. By evening he is back checking moisture levels, worried that his own borewells are starting to yield less each season.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Rajesh lives in a pucca house on the edge of Nandi town with his wife, their two sons aged fourteen and ten, and his widowed mother. His wife manages the household budget, the grape accounts and the kitchen garden; she also works harvest season in the vines alongside hired labourers. His mother looks after the younger boy when school is out and cooks the midday meal. His elder son finished eighth standard last year at the government high school in Nandi and now travels by KSRTC bus to a private PU college in Chikkaballapur town, a daily commute that costs two hundred rupees a week under the Shakti scheme's free-ride provision. Rajesh had hoped the boy would help more with the drilling work during weekends, but his wife insists he focus on studies and aim for an engineering seat in Bengaluru. The younger son is in fifth standard at the same government school. Gender roles in the household are conventional: his wife's labour in the fields is essential but unpaid in cash terms, and decisions about land, the rig and major purchases rest with Rajesh, though she vetoes anything that threatens school fees.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Rajesh studied up to tenth standard at the government high school in Nandi, passing his SSLC on the second attempt, then worked on his father's land. His wife completed seventh standard before marriage. Both are determined that their sons will study further. The elder boy's PU college fees are seven thousand rupees per term plus textbooks and exam fees, manageable so far but a stretch if the grape price crashes. The school provides midday meals and the bus ride is free under Shakti, cutting daily costs. Rajesh dreams of an engineering seat for his elder son, ideally through CET quota to avoid capitation fees, knowing that a degree could mean a Bengaluru IT job and escape from the borewell lottery. The younger boy is doing well in Kannada medium; Rajesh sometimes wonders whether English medium would have been better but cannot afford the private school fees others pay. He worries that if grape income falls or if he has a bad drilling season, keeping the elder boy in college will mean taking another loan.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Rajesh's family draws water from a borewell on their plot, and like most in Nandi taluk they know the water is high in fluoride. His mother has dental fluorosis, brown-stained teeth that the anganwadi worker says comes from decades of the same water. His younger son had white patches on his teeth noticed during a school dental camp two years ago; the visiting doctor advised reverse-osmosis filtration or piped supply, neither of which Rajesh has managed yet. Jal Jeevan Mission taps were promised but not yet installed in their ward in 2025. The family goes to the government primary health centre in Nandi for fever and minor injuries; for anything serious they travel to Chikkaballapur district hospital or, if they can afford it, a private clinic in Chikkaballapur town. His wife had both sons delivered at the government taluk hospital with JSY assistance. Rajesh himself has chronic back pain from years of manual rig work and sometimes takes painkillers bought from the town pharmacy. Heat exhaustion is a risk in summer drilling work. He worries most about an accident with the rig or a snakebite in the fields, knowing ambulance response from Nandi is slow.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Rajesh's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, the dominant landowning group in this part of Chikkaballapur. They are Hindu, observing festivals like Ugadi, Varamahalakshmi and Deepavali, and his mother insists on visiting the Bhoga Nandeeshwara Temple at the foot of Nandi Hills at least once a year. Rajesh sometimes joins the annual jatre at the hilltop Yoga Nandeeshwara shrine when drilling work permits. Community ties matter for labour-sharing during harvest and for contracts: several of his drilling customers are Vokkaliga neighbours or relatives who trust him to deliver an honest depth report even when the borewell fails. Caste plays out in unspoken ways in land ownership and access to credit; the SC families in Nandi's outlying hamlets are more likely to work as wage labourers than own rigs or vines. Rajesh is not deeply religious but respects his mother's daily puja routine and the annual household festivals. The local Hanuman temple is a gathering point for men in the evening. He has heard of Siddaganga Mutt's free hostels but his family has not needed that help so far.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He has not seen Yettinahole water yet and does not expect it soon, but Shakti has saved his family real money on his son's college commute. He interacted with the gram panchayat to get his house connected to the rural electrification line and again when the MGNREGA work-site near his plot needed coordination. He is sceptical of officials: the promised Jal Jeevan Mission tap has not arrived, and the soil-testing camp announced for grape farmers last year never materialised. His borewell rig is licensed and he pays motor-vehicle tax, but drilling itself is unregulated and he knows some contractors give false depth reports to get paid faster. He has taken crop loans from the cooperative bank and once queued for drought-relief compensation after a failed monsoon. The Chikkaballapur RTO, taluk office and mandi are the government touchpoints he knows best. He respects local leaders who can deliver a road or a transformer but dismisses most taluk politics as family theatre.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Rajesh is proud of coaxing a living from dry land through hard work, drip irrigation and the calculated risk of his drilling business. He worries most about water: that his own borewells are yielding less, that clients blame him when new borewells fail, and that the whole grape belt may become unviable if the water table keeps falling. He resents that Chikkaballapur is so close to Bengaluru's wealth and Kempegowda Airport's land boom, yet his taluk still lacks assured piped water and his children must commute for decent schooling. He blames successive governments for promising Yettinahole and delivering little, though he does not trust the Malnad objectors either. Grape price crashes make him angry at commission agents and the unregulated market; he wants a minimum support price or cooperative processing to stabilise income. He is proud his elder son is in college and determined the boy will not inherit the borewell-dependence trap. He dislikes being lumped with "backward interior Karnataka" when Nandi is an hour from the airport, yet he knows the airport corridor's land speculators are not his friends. He wants his sons educated, his water secure and recognition that bayalu seeme farmers feed Bengaluru while getting little back.
